0.title: 3 John: Walking in Truth, Tested by Character
0.overview:
Third John is the most personal letter in the New Testament — a private note, fifteen verses, addressed by name to a specific individual. It never quotes the Old Testament, never rises to the theological heights of 1 John, never delivers a formal doctrinal argument. It is, in the best sense, a pastoral letter: warm, direct, full of the texture of real church life, and quietly devastating in its portrait of two men who could not be more different. Gaius receives it with joy; Diotrephes, the elder hopes, will hear of it with something closer to shame.

The author is again “the elder” — the same hand that wrote 2 John, by tradition the last of the apostles, the old man who has outlived everyone and carries in his body and his memory the full weight of what it means to have known Jesus. He writes to a man named Gaius, who is otherwise unknown to us outside this letter but who is clearly a person of some standing in his local congregation — hospitable, faithful, generous, walking in the truth. The elder loves him dearly and says so without embarrassment.

The letter’s world is the world of early Christian itinerant mission: travelling teachers and evangelists who moved between house churches, depending entirely on the hospitality of local believers for food, lodging, and a hearing. In 2 John the elder warned against giving that hospitality to false teachers. In 3 John he commends giving it generously to faithful missionaries — and confronts a church leader who has weaponised his position to control the flow of hospitality for his own self-aggrandisement. The two letters are mirror images: together they answer the question of how the church should handle the connection between hospitality, authority, and truth.

The character sketch of Diotrephes is one of the most memorable in the New Testament — a man who “loves to be first,” who refuses the elder’s authority, who drives out members who show hospitality to the missionaries. He is not a false teacher in the doctrinal sense. He is something perhaps more common and more dangerous: a man of genuine religious position who has confused the authority of his office with the authority of his person, and who uses the machinery of the church to serve his own pre-eminence. The elder names him publicly, without rancour, with devastating precision.

1.title: Truth, Hospitality, and the Test of Character
1.overview:
The single chapter of 3 John moves through five movements with the elder’s characteristic economy. The greeting (vv. 1–2) establishes the pastoral relationship and prays for the health of a beloved friend. The commendation (vv. 3–4) celebrates what the elder has heard about Gaius — he is walking in the truth — and names this as the elder’s greatest joy. The appeal (vv. 5–8) calls Gaius to continue his faithful hospitality to the travelling missionaries who have brought news of him to the elder’s community. The confrontation (vv. 9–12) names Diotrephes and his behaviour, and commends Demetrius as the counterexample. And the closing (vv. 13–15) defers the fuller conversation to the face-to-face visit, with greetings from the friends by name.

The letter’s great theme is the inseparability of truth and character. Walking in the truth (vv. 3–4) is not merely holding correct doctrine; it is living in such a way that the truth is visible in how you treat people, especially people who have come to you in the name of the gospel with nothing but a letter of introduction. Gaius demonstrates the truth by how he opens his home. Diotrephes denies the truth — not in his creed but in his conduct — by how he closes his heart. The difference between the two men is the difference between a life shaped by the gospel and a life shaped by the desire for pre-eminence.

The portrait of Diotrephes is the letter’s most searching pastoral gift. He is not a heretic. He is not an immoral man in any conventional sense. He is a man who has placed himself first in a community that belongs to Christ — and in doing so has made the community his own instrument rather than the Lord’s. The church has known men like Diotrephes in every century. The letter’s willingness to name him, to describe his behaviour precisely, and to call his conduct “evil” is itself a form of pastoral courage that every generation of church leaders needs to see modelled.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The greeting is intimate in a way that none of the other Johannine letters quite achieves. The elder writes to a specific man, whom he loves personally (“whom I love in truth” — the same phrase as the opening of 2 John, but there addressed to a community; here addressed to one man). The love is genuine, sustained, personal. The elder does not merely respect Gaius; he loves him. And the love is “in truth” — it is not merely an emotional attachment but a love grounded in and shaped by the shared truth of the gospel. This is the quality of relationship that the gospel creates: not a professional connection, not a formal religious bond, but something closer to family.

The prayer of v. 2 — “I pray that all may go well with you and that you may be in good health, as it goes well with your soul” — is the only prayer in the New Testament that explicitly addresses physical health alongside spiritual wellbeing. The elder uses the state of Gaius’s soul as the measure of his prayer for everything else: may your outer life be as flourishing as your inner life. It is a profound and unexpected compliment. The implication is that Gaius’s soul is doing well — and this is not a given; it is notable enough to serve as a standard. His walking in truth is not merely an outward performance; it is the health of the whole man.

The word “beloved” (agapētos) with which the elder addresses Gaius here and in vv. 5, 11 anchors the whole letter in the love that is the elder’s most consistent theological theme. This is the same word used in 1 John 4:7 (“Beloved, let us love one another”) and throughout his writings. The pastoral relationship the elder has with Gaius is itself an instance of the love that the elder has spent his life commending. He is not merely teaching about love; he is practising it.
verseByVerse.theology:
Love in Truth

The elder loves Gaius in truth and prays that all may go well with him as it goes well with his soul.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Gaius’s soul was healthy enough to be the measure of the prayer.

Now: Pray for the whole person, knowing the soul matters most.

verseByVerse.quote: The elder to the beloved Gaius, whom I love in truth. Beloved, I pray that all may go well with you and that you may be in good health, as it goes well with your soul.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Gaius is a common Latin name — common enough that three or four men named Gaius appear in Paul’s letters and in Acts (Romans 16:23; 1 Corinthians 1:14; Acts 19:29; 20:4). Whether this Gaius is identical with any of them is impossible to determine, and the letter gives us no clues. He is known entirely through this letter — and what it reveals is sufficient: a man of genuine faith, generous hospitality, and a soul that is well.

The phrase “as it goes well with your soul” (kathōs euodoutai sou hē psychē) uses euodoumai, the same verb used in Romans 1:10 for Paul’s prayer that his journey to Rome might “prosper” by God’s will. The implication is that Gaius’s spiritual journey is prospering — it is on the right road, moving in the right direction — and the elder prays that the rest of his life would prosper equally. The soul sets the standard; everything else is measured against it.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The elder has received a report about Gaius from the travelling brothers — faithful missionaries who had visited Gaius’s community and then returned to the elder’s church with the news. The news is that Gaius is walking in the truth. This is not a report about his doctrinal orthodoxy in isolation; the brothers testify to his “faithfulness” — a faithfulness that will be described in vv. 5–8 as the generous hospitality he has shown to strangers who came to him in the name of the gospel. Walking in the truth is not merely believing the right things; it is living them, including living them toward people you have never met.

The joy of v. 4 — “no greater joy than this” — is the same pastoral joy that appears in 2 John 4 and in Paul’s letters to the Thessalonians and Philippians. The faithful pastor’s deepest joy is not his own spiritual achievement, not his own doctrinal clarity, not his own ministerial success. It is the sight of his children walking in the truth. The elder who has spent his life in the service of the gospel, who has outlived his contemporaries, who has watched the deceivers go out — his greatest joy is a man in a distant city opening his home to strangers because they come in the name of Jesus Christ.

The phrase “my children” may mean that Gaius came to faith through the elder’s ministry, or through the wider apostolic mission for which the elder feels parental responsibility. The relationship is not merely collegial; it is familial. The elder is a father in the gospel, and Gaius is his son in the faith. This parental language runs throughout the Johannine letters and Paul’s letters — the apostolic relationship creates a bond that is deeper than professional or institutional, closer to the love that a parent has for the children who carry their life forward.
verseByVerse.theology:
No Greater Joy

Travelling brothers testified to Gaius’s truth. The elder’s greatest joy is hearing that his children walk in the truth.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Gaius’s faithfulness was known by what others experienced of it.

Now: A life that walks in truth leaves traces others can see.

verseByVerse.quote: For I rejoiced greatly when the brothers came and testified to your truth, as indeed you are walking in the truth. I have no greater joy than to hear that my children are walking in the truth.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The brothers who brought the report are almost certainly the same missionaries whom Gaius had received in vv. 5–8 — they had visited Gaius’s community, experienced his hospitality, and returned to the elder’s church with news of him. The report is not about his doctrinal views; it is about the quality of his faithfulness in practice. The brothers “testified to your truth” — your truth, not merely the truth in the abstract. The truth has become personal, embodied, visible in Gaius.

The phrase “no greater joy than this” (meizotera toutōn ouk echō charan) is an absolute superlative — not merely a great joy among many, but the greatest joy. This is remarkable given everything the elder has experienced: the original fellowship with Jesus, the resurrection appearances, Pentecost, a lifetime of apostolic ministry. Yet his definitive statement of greatest joy is this: hearing that his children are walking in the truth. The apostle who wrote the most transcendent Christology in the New Testament names this pastoral joy as the summit.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The appeal of vv. 5–8 is the theological counterpart to the prohibition of 2 John 10–11. There the elder said: do not receive false teachers into your home, because to do so is to participate in their destructive work. Here he says: do receive faithful missionaries into your home, because to do so is to become a fellow worker in the truth. The hospitality that the gospel forbids in one direction, it commands in the other. The same act — opening your home — can be either a betrayal of the gospel or an expression of it, depending entirely on who you are welcoming and why.

Gaius is commended for showing hospitality to “brothers, strangers at that” — men he had never met personally, who probably came to him carrying letters of introduction from the apostolic community. In the first-century world, where public inns were dangerous and disreputable, the practice of providing hospitality to travelling Christians was essential to the mission. The letter of introduction — the epistolē systatikē — was the mechanism by which the community of truth extended its network of care across distances. Gaius received these strangers not because he knew them personally but because he knew whose name they bore.

The missionaries who received Gaius’s hospitality have “gone out for the sake of the name, accepting nothing from the Gentiles” (v. 7). This is the first-century version of faith mission — travelling teachers who refused to accept support from those outside the Christian community, depending entirely on the generosity of the churches they visited. Their refusal to accept Gentile support was a mark of integrity: they were not in it for what they could get from those they ministered to. They came to give, not to receive. Those who support such people, the elder argues, become “fellow workers for the truth” — synergoi tē alētheia, partners in the very work they could not themselves do.
verseByVerse.theology:
Fellow Workers for the Truth

Welcoming faithful missionaries makes the host a fellow worker for the truth. Receiving them is the counterpart of refusing the deceivers in 2 John.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The missionaries took nothing from the Gentiles and relied on the churches.

Now: Those who support gospel workers share their work.

verseByVerse.quote: Beloved, it is a faithful thing you do in all your efforts for these brothers, strangers as they are, who testified to your love before the church. You will do well to send them on their journey in a manner worthy of God. For they have gone out for the sake of the name, accepting nothing from the Gentiles. Therefore we ought to support people like these, that we may be fellow workers for the truth.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The phrase “in a manner worthy of God” (axiōs tou theou) sets the standard for Christian hospitality: not merely adequate, not merely polite, but worthy of the God in whose name the missionaries travel. This same phrase appears in 1 Thessalonians 2:12 (“walk in a manner worthy of God”) and Colossians 1:10 (“walk in a manner worthy of the Lord”). The standard is not what feels comfortable or what is culturally expected; it is what befits someone representing the God who gave his Son for the world.

“Sending them on their journey” (propempsas) is a technical term in the Pauline letters for a specific act of Christian hospitality: not merely providing for the visitor during their stay, but equipping them for the next stage of their journey — provision of food, funds, perhaps companions. Paul uses the same word in Romans 15:24, 1 Corinthians 16:6, and 2 Corinthians 1:16. To “send on the journey” was to take responsibility for the missionary’s transition to their next destination, not merely to bid them farewell at the door.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The confrontation with Diotrephes is the letter’s most arresting passage — the apostle naming a specific person, in a specific community, for a specific pattern of behaviour that is damaging the church’s mission and the elder’s authority. The elder has already written to the church (v. 9 — apparently a letter that Diotrephes has suppressed or ignored), and Diotrephes has rejected his authority. When the elder comes in person, he will deal with what Diotrephes is doing.

The description of Diotrephes is devastating in its precision. He “likes to put himself first” — the Greek is philoprōteuōn, a compound word meaning “one who loves to be first,” and no earlier example of it is known. John may have coined the word to name exactly what Diotrephes is. He does not merely want leadership; he wants pre-eminence. He does not merely exercise authority; he makes himself the centre. He speaks wicked nonsense against the elder with malicious words. He refuses to welcome the brothers. He stops those who want to welcome them — and expels them from the church. Every item on the list is a manifestation of the one root: the love of being first.

The contrast with Gaius could not be more stark. Gaius opened his home to strangers; Diotrephes closed the church’s door. Gaius’s faithfulness is celebrated by the brothers; Diotrephes’s behaviour is reported to the elder. Gaius is a fellow worker for the truth; Diotrephes is actively obstructing it. Both are in positions of some standing within the community — but position does not determine character. The letter makes clear that the truth about a person is revealed not by the office they hold but by what they do with it.

Demetrius (v. 12) is the counterexample — and possibly the bearer of this letter. He has testimony from everyone, from the truth itself, and from the elder. The triple testimony is John’s pattern of establishing certainty (cf. 1 John 5:7–8 on the three witnesses). Demetrius is the kind of person Gaius should welcome — and possibly the kind of person Diotrephes will attempt to turn away. The letter functions as a pre-emptive endorsement: when Demetrius arrives, receive him.
verseByVerse.theology:
Diotrephes and Demetrius

Diotrephes loves to be first; he rejects the elder, refuses the brothers and expels those who welcome them. Imitate good, not evil.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Demetrius had a good testimony from everyone and from the truth itself.

Now: The love of being first shows itself in whom it shuts out.

verseByVerse.quote: I have written something to the church, but Diotrephes, who likes to put himself first, does not acknowledge our authority. So if I come, I will bring up what he is doing, talking wicked nonsense against us. And not content with that, he refuses to welcome the brothers, and also stops those who want to and puts them out of the church.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The verb philoprōteuōn (“likes to put himself first”) occurs only here in the New Testament, and no earlier example is known. John appears to have coined it to name exactly what Diotrephes is. This is not the ordinary ambition that marks a leader; it is the pathological desire for pre-eminence that makes every relationship — with the elder, with the brothers, with members of the congregation — a contest for the first position. Jesus had addressed exactly this spirit among his own disciples: “whoever would be first among you must be your slave” (Matthew 20:27; cf. Mark 9:35). Diotrephes has chosen the opposite path.

The elder’s earlier letter to the church (v. 9) is not otherwise known — it has not survived, and we cannot determine its contents. What we know is that Diotrephes suppressed it or dismissed it: “does not acknowledge our authority.” The Greek is ouk epidechetai hēmas — does not receive us, does not accept us. The same verb appears in v. 10 for Diotrephes’s refusal to “welcome” the brothers. He refuses both the apostolic authority and the apostolic missionaries. The two refusals are the same act at different levels.

verseByVerse.quote: Beloved, do not imitate evil but imitate good. Whoever does good is from God; whoever does evil has not seen God. Demetrius has received a good testimony from everyone, and from the truth itself. We also add our testimony, and you know that our testimony is true.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The instruction to “imitate” (mimou) good rather than evil is the letter’s pastoral pivot: faced with the contrasting examples of Gaius, Diotrephes, and Demetrius, the reader is invited not merely to observe but to choose which to imitate. The Greek word mimou gives us our word “mimic” — but in the New Testament the concept of imitation is a serious moral category (cf. 1 Corinthians 11:1, “be imitators of me, as I am of Christ”; Hebrews 13:7, “imitate their faith”). Character is formed by whom we model ourselves on; the question is which model we are actually following.

The triple testimony to Demetrius is structured like a legal or covenantal witness: (1) from everyone — the whole community that knows him; (2) from the truth itself — his life is so consistent with the gospel that the truth itself testifies to him; (3) from the elder — the apostolic authority adds its voice. The phrase “you know that our testimony is true” echoes the closing of the Gospel of John (21:24), where the same claim is made about the Beloved Disciple’s testimony. John stakes his full apostolic authority on the commendation of Demetrius.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The closing of 3 John is almost identical to the closing of 2 John — the elder has more to say than ink and paper can carry, he hopes to come soon and speak face to face, the friends send greetings by name. The verbal parallels are so close that the two letters were probably written at roughly the same time, possibly sent together to different communities in the same region. They are companion pieces: 2 John is the warning about false hospitality; 3 John is the commendation of faithful hospitality. Together they answer the same question from two different directions.

The personal greeting of v. 15 — “greet the friends by name” — is unique in the New Testament epistolary tradition. Paul greets people by name in Romans 16 and elsewhere, but he is the one doing the naming. Here the elder delegates the naming to Gaius: greet the friends there by name, as the friends here greet you. It is as if the elder is acknowledging that Gaius knows the community better than he does — knows who is there, who needs to be greeted personally, who carries the weight of a named acknowledgement. The apostle defers to the local shepherd for the personal touch.

The word “peace” (eirēnē) that closes the letter carries the full biblical sense of peace — the wholeness, the completeness, the right-ordered life that flows from being at peace with God. In a letter that has navigated the tensions of conflicting authority, the danger of false teaching, and the damage done by a self-promoting leader, the closing word of peace is not naive optimism. It is the elder’s confident declaration: the God of truth is the God of peace, and those who walk in his truth will find his peace sustaining them through every conflict.
verseByVerse.theology:
Face to Face, and Peace

The elder hopes to speak in person. He sends peace, and asks Gaius to greet the friends each by name.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: 2 and 3 John read as companion letters on hospitality.

Now: The church is a fellowship of friends known by name.

verseByVerse.quote: I had much to write to you, but I would rather not write with pen and ink. I hope to see you soon, and we will talk face to face. Peace be to you. The friends greet you. Greet the friends, each by name.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The closing greeting “peace be to you” is in the singular — addressed to Gaius personally, not to the congregation. The letter began as a personal letter (singular “to you” throughout), and it closes as it began. The whole letter has been a conversation between the elder and one beloved man. The peace pronounced is the peace of a father speaking to a faithful son at the end of a difficult conversation: you have done well; you will face difficulty; peace be with you.

The instruction to greet the friends “each by name” (kat’ onoma) is the final and most intimate detail of this most intimate letter. Each person in the community is known by name — not as a member of a group, not as a representative of a type, but as an individual known and loved by the God who calls his own sheep by name (John 10:3). The elder who has loved Gaius by name, who has confronted Diotrephes by name, who has commended Demetrius by name, closes by asking Gaius to do the same for every person in his community. This is the pastoral vocation in miniature: to know the sheep, each by name.
